definition: In linguistics, Heaps's law (sometimes spelled as Heaps' law), also called Herdan's law, is an empirical law which describes the number of distinct words in a document (or set of documents) as a function of the document length (so called type-token relation).
details: It can be formulated as V R ( n ) = K n β {\displaystyle V_{R}(n)=Kn^{\beta }} where VR is the number of distinct words in an instance text of size n. K and β are free parameters determined empirically. With English text corpora, typically K is between 10 and 100, and β is between 0.4 and 0.6. The law is frequently attributed to Harold Stanley Heaps, but was originally discovered by Gustav Herdan (1960). Under mild assumptions, the Herdan–Heaps law is asymptotically equivalent to Zipf's law concerning the frequencies of individual words within a text. This is a consequence of the fact that the type-token relation (in general) of a homogenous text can be derived from the distribution of its types. Empirically, Heaps's law is preserved even when the document is randomly shuffled, meaning that it does not depend on the ordering of words, but only the frequency of words. This is used as evidence for deriving Heaps's law from Zipf's law. Heaps's law means that as more instance text is gathered, there will be diminishing returns in terms of discovery of the full vocabulary from which the distinct terms are drawn. Deviations from Heaps's law, as typically observed in English text corpora, have been identified in corpora generated with large language models. Heaps's law also applies to situations in which the "vocabulary" is just some set of distinct types which are attributes of some collection of objects. For example, the objects could be people, and the types could be country of origin of the person. If persons are selected randomly (that is, we are not selecting based on country of origin), then Heaps's law says we will quickly have representatives from most countries (in proportion to their population) but it will become increasingly difficult to cover the entire set of countries by continuing this method of sampling. Heaps's law has been observed also in single-cell transcriptomes considering genes as the distinct objects in the "vocabulary".

explainer.lead: Heaps's law says that as a text gets longer, new distinct words appear at an ever-slower rate. It offers a simple description of vocabulary growth and explains why collecting more text brings diminishing returns in uncovering its vocabulary.

tiers.eli5: Imagine collecting stickers: at first, almost every new sticker is different, but later you keep getting ones you already have. Heaps's law describes the same pattern with words in a growing collection of writing. You keep finding new words, but more and more slowly.
tiers.practitioner: For a text corpus, vocabulary growth can be fitted with V_R(n) = K n^β, where n is text length and V_R(n) is the number of distinct words. English corpora typically have K between 10 and 100 and β between 0.4 and 0.6, but these are empirical ranges rather than universal settings. The relationship can persist after random shuffling, and deviations have been observed in corpora generated by large language models.
tiers.paperLevel: Heaps's law, also called Herdan's law, is V_R(n) = K n^β, with K and β determined empirically; English text corpora typically have 10 < K < 100 and 0.4 < β < 0.6. Although frequently attributed to Harold Stanley Heaps, it was originally discovered by Gustav Herdan in 1960. Under mild assumptions, the Herdan–Heaps law is asymptotically equivalent to Zipf's law, and its preservation under random shuffling supports derivation from word frequencies rather than word order. Deviations from the typical English-corpus behaviour have been identified in corpora generated with large language models.

explainer.example: Suppose K = 20 and β = 0.5. A text of 100 words gives V_R(100) = 20 × 100^0.5 = 200 distinct words, while a text of 10,000 words gives V_R(10,000) = 20 × 10,000^0.5 = 2,000. Making the text 100 times longer therefore produces only 10 times as many distinct words under this fitted relationship.

explainer.intuition: Common words recur often, so additional text increasingly repeats vocabulary already seen. Distinct words therefore grow more slowly than the text itself, making the remaining vocabulary progressively harder to uncover.
howItWorks: Take an instance text of size n.
Count its distinct words to obtain V_R(n).
Fit K and β empirically in V_R(n) = K n^β.
Because β is typically below 1, vocabulary grows more slowly than text length.
Expect diminishing returns in discovering new distinct terms as n increases.
explainer.whyItMatters: The law makes vocabulary growth predictable in simple empirical terms and quantifies the diminishing returns of gathering more text. It also connects vocabulary growth to Zipf's law and applies beyond words to other collections of distinct types, including countries of origin and genes.
misconceptions: It does not depend on word ordering: it can remain intact after a document is randomly shuffled.
Its parameters are not universal constants; K and β are determined empirically.
Although often attributed to Harold Stanley Heaps, it was originally discovered by Gustav Herdan in 1960.
